title: Best Medicine for a Hangover: What to Take for Each Symptom
excerpt: There's no single hangover cure, but the right over-the-counter medicine can ease each symptom. Which pain reliever, antacid, or anti-nausea option to take, and what to avoid after drinking.
metaDescription: The best medicine for a hangover depends on your symptom. Which pain reliever, antacid, or anti-nausea option to take after drinking, and what to avoid.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no single medicine that fixes a hangover. A hangover is a bundle of different problems (headache, an upset stomach, nausea, poor sleep, mild dehydration, and the leftover effects of alcohol's by-products), and each over-the-counter medicine only touches one of them. The best medicine for a hangover is the one that matches your worst symptom, taken at the right time and in the right dose. For most healthy adults that means a single dose of an anti-inflammatory pain reliever with food for a headache, an antacid for heartburn, or an anti-nausea option for a queasy stomach. Fluids, food, and time do the heavy lifting.

The catch is that alcohol changes how several of these medicines behave. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol both lean on the liver. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach lining that alcohol has already irritated. Sedating antihistamines stack with alcohol's own drowsiness. This guide walks through each option, what it actually does, and where the risks are.

> **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first if** you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems (including ulcers or reflux), take blood thinners, blood pressure medicine, antidepressants, or any prescription drug, or are pregnant. This article explains general label guidance and research. It is not medical advice. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, has bluish or very pale skin, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and no pill will help. If you think someone took too much of a medicine, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## Quick Picks: Which Hangover Medicine for Which Symptom

| Main symptom | Over-the-counter option to consider | Main caution after drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Headache, body aches | Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve), with food | Stomach irritation and bleeding risk; kidney strain when dehydrated |
| Headache, but your stomach is upset | Acetaminophen (Tylenol), one standard dose after eating and once the alcohol has cleared | Liver strain; hidden acetaminophen in other products |
| Heartburn, acid stomach | Calcium carbonate (Tums) or famotidine (Pepcid) | Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines; Tums can interfere with absorbing some drugs |
| Nausea | Dimenhydrinate (Dramamine), meclizine, or a phosphorated carbohydrate solution (Emetrol) | Antihistamines cause drowsiness; wait until alcohol is out of your system |
| Upset stomach plus diarrhea | Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) | Contains a salicylate (aspirin relative); don't combine with aspirin |
| Diarrhea alone | Loperamide (Imodium), label dose only | Never exceed the label dose |
| Thirst, dizziness, dry mouth | An oral rehydration solution | Not a medicine, but often the most useful item on this list |

Pick one product per problem, read every label, and don't layer several multi-symptom products on top of each other. That's how people end up taking twice the acetaminophen or aspirin they meant to.

## Why There's No Single "Hangover Medicine"

Researchers still don't fully agree on what causes a hangover, which is part of why nothing treats it all at once. The main contributors appear to be:

- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and levels of inflammatory signaling molecules tend to rise during a hangover. This is likely behind much of the headache, achiness, and "flu-like" feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde and other by-products.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. Darker drinks also carry more congeners, by-products of fermentation that seem to make hangovers worse.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Much of next-day fatigue is simply sleep loss.
- **Stomach and gut irritation.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and irritates the stomach lining, which drives nausea, heartburn, and sometimes diarrhea.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol makes you urinate more. Dehydration is real, but research suggests it's a contributor rather than the whole story.
- **Low blood sugar.** Drinking can lower blood sugar, especially if you skipped a meal, which adds to shakiness and weakness.

A pain reliever works on the inflammation and headache. An antacid works on acid. Nothing in the pharmacy speeds up how fast your body clears acetaldehyde or repairs your sleep. That's why systematic reviews of hangover remedies, including a 2005 review in the *BMJ* and a 2021 review in the journal *Addiction*, concluded that there is no good evidence that any remedy reliably prevents or cures hangovers. Those reviews focused on supplements and specific remedies, but the same logic applies to drugstore medicines: they treat symptoms, not the hangover itself.

## Best Medicine for a Hangover Headache

The headache is the symptom most people reach for a pill to fix. You have two families to choose from, and they carry different risks after drinking.

### Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs)

**How they work:** nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block enzymes (called COX enzymes) that make prostaglandins, chemical messengers that drive pain and inflammation. Since hangovers seem to involve inflammation, this is a reasonable match for the headache and body aches. Ibuprofen is the one most people use. Naproxen (Aleve) lasts longer per dose. Aspirin works in a similar way.

**The interaction with alcohol:** prostaglandins also help protect the stomach lining. When an NSAID lowers them, the stomach becomes more vulnerable to acid. Alcohol already raises stomach acid and irritates the lining, so the two together raise the risk of irritation, ulcers, and bleeding. That's why the FDA-required label on over-the-counter NSAIDs carries a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product. NSAIDs can also reduce blood flow to the kidneys, which matters more when you're dehydrated.

**How to use them more safely after drinking:**

- Take a single label dose with food and a full glass of water.
- Skip them if your stomach is already burning or painful, or if you've been vomiting.
- Don't take two NSAIDs together (for example, ibuprofen plus aspirin or naproxen).
- Avoid them if you've had ulcers or stomach bleeding, have kidney disease, take blood thinners, or have been told to avoid them for heart reasons.

Our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol), [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol), and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) go deeper on each one.

### Acetaminophen (Tylenol)

**How it works:** acetaminophen relieves pain and fever through the brain and spinal cord, and it does very little for inflammation. It's gentle on the stomach, which is its main advantage after a rough night.

**The interaction with alcohol:** your liver breaks down most of each acetaminophen dose safely, but a small part is turned into a toxic by-product called NAPQI. The liver neutralizes NAPQI with an antioxidant called glutathione. Regular heavy drinking increases the enzyme that makes NAPQI and drains glutathione, and fasting lowers glutathione further. When NAPQI builds up faster than it can be cleared, liver cells are damaged. Acetaminophen is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, and many of those cases are accidental: a little too much over a few days, often from more than one product, often alongside alcohol. The FDA-required label tells people who have 3 or more drinks every day to ask a doctor before using it.

**How to use it more safely after drinking:**

- Never take it before bed "to get ahead of" a hangover. Wait until the alcohol has cleared.
- Eat first, then take one standard dose rather than a stack.
- Count every source. Acetaminophen hides in NyQuil, DayQuil, Tylenol PM, Excedrin, many cold and flu products, and some prescription painkillers. Look for "acetaminophen," "APAP," or "paracetamol" in the Drug Facts box.
- If you drink heavily most days, talk to a doctor before using it at all.

Read the full breakdown in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

### So which pain reliever is best for a hangover?

For an occasional drinker whose only real problem is a headache, ibuprofen with food is usually the better fit, because it targets inflammation and spares the liver. If your stomach is the bigger problem (heartburn, pain, vomiting), acetaminophen taken later in the day after eating is often gentler, as long as you don't drink heavily on a regular basis and you keep to one dose. Neither is a good idea in large or repeated doses. Our [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) comparison walks through the decision in more detail, and our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the non-drug steps that help too.

### What about Excedrin and Alka-Seltzer?

These are combination products, so check what's inside. Excedrin Extra Strength combines acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine, which means it carries both the liver warning and the stomach-bleeding warning (see [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol)). Original Alka-Seltzer is aspirin with baking soda and citric acid, so it's an NSAID with an antacid attached, and it's high in sodium. The Alka-Seltzer brand also sells products with entirely different ingredients, so read the specific box rather than trusting the name.

## Best Medicine for Hangover Heartburn and Acid Stomach

Alcohol relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach and increases acid, which is why the morning after can come with a burning chest or a sour stomach.

- **Calcium carbonate (Tums)** neutralizes acid that's already there. It works within minutes and is a simple first choice. It can interfere with absorbing some medicines (certain antibiotics and thyroid medicine, for example), so space it out from other pills and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure. See [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol).
- **Famotidine (Pepcid)** lowers acid production for longer, roughly half a day. It's a reasonable choice if the heartburn keeps coming back. Some older acid reducers in the same class were found to raise blood alcohol levels slightly, which is one reason to take acid medicine after drinking rather than as a way to drink more comfortably. Famotidine appears to have little of that effect, but the principle holds.
- **Avoid adding an NSAID** if your stomach is burning. That combination is exactly what the stomach-bleeding warning is about.

If heartburn after drinking is a regular thing for you, our [heartburn after drinking guide](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains the triggers and what tends to help.

## Best Medicine for Hangover Nausea

Nausea is the symptom people find hardest to push through, and it can stop you from drinking the fluids you need.

- **Dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) and meclizine** are antihistamines usually sold for motion sickness. They can ease nausea, but they also make you drowsy, and alcohol is a sedative too. Only use them once the alcohol is out of your system, and don't drive afterward. See [Dramamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol).
- **Phosphorated carbohydrate solution (Emetrol)** is a sugar-based liquid that calms the stomach without making you sleepy. It isn't suitable for people with diabetes because of the sugar content.
- **Ondansetron (Zofran)** is a prescription anti-nausea medicine. Some urgent care and IV clinics use it for persistent vomiting. If you have it prescribed for another reason, check with the prescriber before using it after drinking. Our [Zofran and alcohol](/never-hungover/zofran-and-alcohol) page covers the details.
- **Ginger** isn't a drug, but it has modest evidence for nausea in other settings, and ginger tea or chews are a gentle first step. See [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover).

Sip small amounts of water or an oral rehydration drink every few minutes rather than gulping. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more practical steps.

## Best Medicine for an Upset Stomach and Diarrhea After Drinking

Alcohol speeds up the gut and irritates its lining, which is why diarrhea after a night out is so common.

- **Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol)** coats and calms the stomach and can help with nausea, indigestion, and diarrhea all at once. The "salicylate" part is related to aspirin, so don't take it with aspirin, and be cautious if you take blood thinners or are allergic to aspirin. It can turn your tongue and stool black. That's harmless, but it can hide the black, tarry stool that signals bleeding in the stomach, so keep that in mind. See [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol).
- **Loperamide (Imodium)** slows the gut and is effective for simple diarrhea. Stick strictly to the label dose. The FDA has warned that taking much more than the recommended amount can cause serious heart rhythm problems.

If you have a fever, blood in your stool, or diarrhea that lasts more than a couple of days, that's no longer a hangover and needs a doctor.

## What About Fatigue, Dehydration, and Sleep?

There's no pill for the tired, foggy feeling, and some of the things people reach for make it worse.

- **Rehydrate with something that has salt in it.** An oral rehydration solution replaces sodium and potassium along with water. Plain water is fine too, especially with a salty snack. Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) explains what's actually in each.
- **Coffee is fine in moderation.** If you normally drink coffee, having your usual cup prevents a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. Too much can upset your stomach and make anxiety and shakiness worse.
- **Skip sleep aids with alcohol in your system.** Diphenhydramine (the antihistamine in Benadryl, ZzzQuil, and most "PM" products) and doxylamine (in NyQuil and Unisom SleepTabs) stack with alcohol's sedation. Some PM products also contain acetaminophen. Our [Benadryl for hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) page covers this.
- **Never mix alcohol with prescription sedatives** such as benzodiazepines or sleeping pills unless your doctor has specifically told you it's safe. The combination can slow breathing dangerously.
- **Eat something.** Toast, crackers, eggs, or soup bring blood sugar back up and give your stomach something besides acid to work on.

## Hangover Medicine Mistakes to Avoid

These are the patterns that turn a bad morning into a real medical problem:

1. **Taking a pain reliever before bed "just in case."** You add liver or stomach strain while alcohol is still being processed, and there's no good evidence it prevents the morning headache.
2. **Doubling up on hidden ingredients.** A Tylenol for your head, NyQuil to sleep, and a cold tablet the next day can add up to far more acetaminophen than you meant to take. Read every Drug Facts box.
3. **Mixing NSAIDs.** Ibuprofen plus aspirin, or Aleve plus Alka-Seltzer, piles up stomach risk without adding much relief.
4. **Treating vomiting with more pills.** If you can't keep water down, an oral pill won't stay down either, and an empty, irritated stomach is the worst place for an NSAID.
5. **Using a hangover as a reason to take something stronger.** Leftover prescription painkillers, muscle relaxants, or anxiety medicine don't belong in a hangover routine.
6. **"Hair of the dog."** Another drink delays the hangover rather than treating it, and it adds to the load on your liver.

## Build a Simple Hangover Medicine Kit

If you want something ready for the morning after a wedding or a big night, keep it short:

- One pain reliever you know suits you (ibuprofen for most occasional drinkers, or acetaminophen if NSAIDs bother your stomach)
- An antacid such as Tums
- An oral rehydration drink or electrolyte powder
- Something bland to eat
- Ginger chews or tea

That covers most of what a hangover throws at you without stacking interactions. For more ideas, see our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas). Store medicines in their original packaging so the label and dosing information are always with them.

## When to See a Doctor

For a social drinker, a normal hangover peaks in the morning and fades over the day, and most people feel close to normal within about 24 hours. Get medical care if you notice any of these:

- **Signs of alcohol poisoning** in anyone who's been drinking: confusion, being hard to wake, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, very pale or bluish skin, or low body temperature. Call 911 and don't leave the person alone.
- **Vomiting that won't stop**, or not being able to keep any fluids down for many hours, especially with dizziness or very little urine.
- **Vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds**, or **black, tarry stool** (remember Pepto-Bismol can blacken stool harmlessly, but don't assume that's the cause).
- **Severe stomach pain**, particularly pain that spreads to the back, or pain under the right ribs.
- **Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle**, or fainting.
- **Yellowing of the skin or eyes**, dark urine, or easy bruising after taking acetaminophen.
- **Any chance you took too much of a medicine.** Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) even if you feel fine, because acetaminophen overdose can look mild for the first day.
- **Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, or seeing or hearing things a day or two after you stop drinking**, if you've been drinking heavily every day. That can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it can become dangerous. Tell a doctor plainly what you've been drinking so they can treat it safely.
- **Hangovers that last more than a day**, keep getting worse, or come with symptoms you don't usually get.

A pharmacist is also a good, free first stop. They can look at the medicines you already take and tell you which hangover option is safe for you.

## Do Hangover Pills and Supplements Work?

The supplement aisle is full of products sold as hangover cures. Some contain vitamins and electrolytes, some contain plant extracts, and a few contain acetaminophen or aspirin without making that obvious on the front of the box. Reviews of the research, including the *BMJ* and *Addiction* reviews mentioned earlier, have found that the studies behind most hangover remedies are small and low in quality, and there is no good evidence that any of them reliably prevents or cures a hangover. We cover the individual claims in [do hangover pills actually work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work).

One ingredient that comes up often is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Lab and animal studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and may support the liver, and there is a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and it does not make it safe to combine alcohol with acetaminophen or NSAIDs. Some people like to take it with water before or during a night out as part of a broader routine that also includes eating, pacing drinks, and hydrating. If you want to try it, a well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and a higher-priced blend that adds L-cysteine and electrolytes is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Check our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) if you take any prescription medicine, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for how much people typically use.

The most reliable "medicine" is still the unglamorous one: fewer drinks, more water, food in your stomach, and enough sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- No medicine cures a hangover. Match the medicine to your worst symptom and keep it to one product per problem.
- For a headache, ibuprofen or naproxen with food is usually the better fit for an occasional drinker. Acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach but adds work for the liver, so wait until the alcohol has cleared and take one standard dose.
- For heartburn, use an antacid like Tums or an acid reducer like famotidine, and skip NSAIDs if your stomach is burning.
- For nausea, consider Dramamine or meclizine once the alcohol is gone, or a non-drowsy option like Emetrol, plus small sips of fluid.
- Don't take pain relievers before bed "just in case," don't combine sleep aids with alcohol, and read every Drug Facts box for hidden acetaminophen and aspirin.
- If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, or have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using any of these.
- Signs of alcohol poisoning, blood in vomit or stool, or severe pain need medical care, not more medicine.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best medicine for a hangover?**

There is no single medicine that treats a whole hangover. The best approach is to match the medicine to your worst symptom: an anti-inflammatory pain reliever such as ibuprofen (taken with food) for a headache, an antacid such as Tums for heartburn, and an antihistamine motion-sickness pill or a sugar-based anti-nausea liquid for queasiness. Fluids, food, and sleep do the rest. If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have liver, stomach, or kidney problems, or take other medicines, ask a pharmacist or doctor which option is safe for you.

**Is ibuprofen or Tylenol better for a hangover?**

For an occasional drinker who feels fine apart from a headache, ibuprofen taken with food and water is usually the better match, because hangovers involve inflammation and acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds work for the liver after drinking. Ibuprofen is harder on the stomach, though, so skip it if you have heartburn, stomach pain, ulcers, kidney disease, or take blood thinners. Neither is a good idea in large or repeated doses after heavy drinking.

**Can I take medicine before bed after drinking to prevent a hangover?**

It's better not to. Taking acetaminophen while alcohol is still in your system adds strain on the liver, and taking an NSAID like ibuprofen or aspirin on top of a stomach that alcohol has already irritated raises the risk of irritation and bleeding. Drink water and go to sleep. If you wake up with a headache, eat something first and then take a single standard dose of the pain reliever that suits you.

**What medicine helps hangover nausea?**

Over-the-counter options include dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) or meclizine, which are antihistamines that calm nausea but cause drowsiness, so only take them once the alcohol has worn off and you don't need to drive. A phosphorated carbohydrate solution sold as Emetrol is a non-drowsy option. Ginger has modest evidence for nausea in general. Prescription ondansetron (Zofran) is sometimes used for persistent vomiting. If you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, or you vomit blood, get medical help.

**Is Pepto-Bismol good for a hangover?**

Pepto-Bismol can help an upset stomach, nausea, and diarrhea after drinking. Its active ingredient, bismuth subsalicylate, is related to aspirin, so don't take it together with aspirin or other salicylates, and be careful if you take blood thinners or are allergic to aspirin. It can also turn your tongue and stool black, which is harmless but can hide the black, tarry stool that signals stomach bleeding.

**Is Alka-Seltzer a good hangover medicine?**

Original Alka-Seltzer contains aspirin, so it works on headache and settles acid with baking soda, but it carries the same stomach-bleeding warning as other aspirin products for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. It's also high in sodium. Check the box carefully, because different Alka-Seltzer products contain very different ingredients, including some with acetaminophen.

**Can I take NyQuil or a sleep aid for a hangover?**

It's best not to combine them with alcohol in your system. NyQuil and many "PM" products contain acetaminophen plus a sedating antihistamine, so they add to liver load and stack drowsiness on top of alcohol. Alcohol also already disrupts sleep. If you can't sleep after drinking, wait it out with water and a dark, cool room rather than reaching for a sleeping pill.

**Do hangover pills or DHM work?**

There is no good evidence that any pill cures a hangover. Systematic reviews of hangover remedies have found the quality of the research to be low. DHM (dihydromyricetin) has interesting lab and animal research on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with limited human data, so it's reasonable to see it as promising but unproven. It isn't a substitute for drinking less, and it doesn't make it safe to combine alcohol with acetaminophen or NSAIDs.
